links.note: 334 says what shows itself as a 'day' (நாளென ஒன்றுபோற் காட்டி) is a blade that saws through life (உயிர் ஈரும் வாள்), for those who perceive it. 1221 has the parted woman tell the hour it is not evening (மாலையோ அல்லை) but a thing that eats the life of those once wed (உயிருண்ணும் வேலை; Parimelazhagar takes வேலை as a final hour, Manakkudavar and Kalaignar as a spear). Both unmask a unit of time as something that consumes life, one as a general truth of impermanence, the other as one lover's experience of separation.

326 calls Death 'the life-eating' (உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று) and says it does not advance on the days of one who does not kill. 1221 gives the same epithet, உயிருண்ணும், to the evening that comes on women parted from their husbands. The pairing shows the woman addressing evening in the book's own language for Death; Parimelazhagar's note on 1229 says she thinks of evening as கூற்றம்.

In 1168 the woman pities the night, which puts all living beings to sleep and has no companion but her (என்னல்லது இல்லை துணை). In 1222 she tells the dim evening it looks sad-eyed (புன்கண்ணை) and asks whether its partner too is hard-eyed like hers (எம்கேள்போல் வன்கண்ணதோ நின் துணை). In both she treats a time of day as a fellow sufferer and asks about its துணை, the one thing she herself lacks.

1223 says the evening that used to come budding with chill and looking wan (பனி அரும்பிப் பைதல்கொள் மாலை) now comes with revulsion budding and sorrow growing (துனி அரும்பித் துன்பம் வளர). 1227 says her sickness buds in the morning (காலை அரும்பி), swells through the day and opens in the evening. Both use அரும்பு, budding, for her pain, and together they give evening as both what brings the bud and when it opens.

1169 says the long nights now passing are crueller than the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய). 1224 says that where her lover is absent (காதலர் இல்வழி) evening comes like ஏதிலர், pitiless strangers or foes, on a killing ground (கொலைக்களத்து). Both make a stretch of time into a cruel agent set beside human cruelty, and 1224 names the condition: it is so only in his absence.

319 states a rule: hurt done to others in the forenoon (முற்பகல்) comes back to oneself in the afternoon (பிற்பகல்), of itself. In 1225 the woman asks what good she did to morning (காலைக்குச் செய்த நன்று) and what enmity she did to evening (மாலைக்குச் செய்த பகை). Her question assumes the same logic of return, that suffering answers something one did, and finds no deed of hers to explain evening's hostility.

In 1083 the man says he did not know before what Death was and now knows (பண்டறியேன் ... இனியறிந்தேன்): it has a woman's nature and warring eyes. In 1226 the woman says that while her husband had not left (மணந்தார் அகலாத காலை) she did not know that evening causes pain (அறிந்ததிலேன்). Both speakers mark love as a before and after in what they know, he at first sight and she at separation.

1147 says this sickness grows long (நீளும் இந் நோய்) with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water. 1227 says this sickness (இந் நோய்) buds in the morning, is a swelling bud all day and blossoms in the evening (காலை அரும்பி ... மாலை மலரும்). Both speak of love's sickness as a plant; 1147 names what feeds it and 1227 gives its daily cycle.

In 1135 the man says the girl has given him the palmyra horse and the anguish suffered at evening (மாலை உழக்கும் துயர்). In 1227 the woman says her sickness blossoms at evening (மாலை மலரும்). The man in courtship and the woman in separation both place the height of love's pain at evening; Parimelazhagar's note on 1135 explains it by saying love blooms at evening, the image of 1227.

66 says only those who have not heard their own children's prattle call the flute sweet (குழல் இனிது). In 1228 the herdsman's flute (ஆயன் குழல்) has become the messenger of the fire-like evening and a weapon that kills (கொல்லும் படை). In both the flute's sweetness depends on the hearer: surpassed for the parent, and turned to pain for the parted woman; Parimelazhagar notes the flute had been sweet to her before.

In 1258 the woman says the soft speech (பணிமொழி) of her deceiving lover is the weapon that breaks her womanly reserve (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை). In 1228 the herdsman's flute is a weapon that kills (கொல்லும் படை). Both call a gentle sound a படை, one because it draws her to him and the other because it announces the evening without him.

In 1168 the night has put all living beings to sleep (மன்னுயிர் எல்லாம் துயிற்றி) and she alone is its companion, so her suffering is solitary. In 1229 she says that when evening spreads, bewildering the mind (மதிமருண்டு; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take this as her own mind), the whole town is bewildered and suffers (பதிமருண்டு பைதல் உழக்கும்). The two speeches picture the world around her in opposite ways, asleep and untouched in one and sharing her distress in the other.

In 1209 the woman says her dear life is perishing (விளியும் என் இன்னுயிர்) as she thinks much on the lack of kindness of one who said they were not separate. In 1230 her life, which had not died till now (மாயா உயிர்), is dying in the dim evening as she thinks of the man whose nature is wealth (பொருள்மாலையாளரை உள்ளி). Both say that thinking of him is what wears her life away, and each names him by a reproach: his broken word in one, his preference for wealth in the other.

In 1263 she says he left desiring victory with his own resolve as companion (உரன் நசைஇ உள்ளம் துணையாகச் சென்றார்), and that she still lives by desiring his return (வரல் நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்). In 1230 thinking of the man given to wealth makes her life die. Both name him by the aim he left for, but in one speech the thought of him keeps her alive and in the other it kills; these are two moments of the same speaker, not a doctrine.

In 1114 the man says that blue lilies, if they could see, would bow and look at the ground, saying they cannot match her eyes (கண்ணொவ்வேம் என்று). In 1231 the friend says that as she thinks of the man gone far, her eyes have grown ashamed before fragrant flowers (நறுமலர் நாணின கண்). Separation reverses the earlier praise: the flowers once shamed by her eyes now shame them, which is how Parimelazhagar glosses 1231.

71 says love cannot be bolted in, because the small tears of the loving make it public (புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்). 1232 says her eyes, pale and running with tears (பசந்து பனிவாரும் கண்), seem to tell of the unkindness of the one she desired (நல்காமை சொல்லுவ போலும்). The same mechanism, tears that disclose, works in both; in 71 they reveal the weeper's love, in 1232 they also accuse the absent lover.

In 1180 the woman says the town easily learns the secret of those like her whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). In 1232 the friend says her pale, weeping eyes seem to be telling of his unkindness. Both treat the eyes as announcing what she would keep hidden; the woman says it of herself and the friend says it to urge her to bear up, as Parimelazhagar frames it.

In 1157 the woman asks whether the bangles slipping past her wrist do not proclaim (தூற்றாகொல்) that the lord of the shore has left her. In 1233 the shoulders that swelled on the day of union (மணந்தநாள் வீங்கிய தோள்) seem to announce fully that he has parted (தணந்தமை சால அறிவிப்ப போலும்). In both her body makes the separation public without her speaking; 1233 adds the contrast with how the same shoulders looked at union.

In 1277 her bangles understood before she did that the lord of the cool shore had parted (தணந்தமை ... முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). In 1233 her shoulders announce that he has parted, with the same word தணந்தமை. In 1277 the body is first to know of the parting, and in 1233 it is the one that tells others.

1234 and 1235 share the line தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள், shoulders whose old beauty has faded. 1234 describes the loss: with her partner gone (துணை நீங்கி) they have lost their fullness and the bangles slip. 1235 turns the same shoulders into testimony that declares the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும்), so the repeated line moves from description to accusation.

In 1262 the woman tells her friend that if she forgets him today (இன்று மறப்பின்), her beauty will leave her shoulders and her ornaments will slip off (கலங்கழியும் காரிகை நீத்து). In 1234 the beauty has faded and the bangles are slipping because her partner is gone (துணை நீங்கி). Read together, the bodily loss follows his absence whether she remembers or forgets, though in 1262 she holds that remembering is what prevents it.

In 1235 the friend, in Parimelazhagar's reading, says the shoulders with bangles lost and old beauty faded declare the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும்). In 1236 the woman answers that with bangles and shoulders slackening, what pains her is the saying that he is cruel (அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). The second verse limits the first: the body's evidence stands, but she refuses the charge drawn from it.

In 1188 the woman complains that people say only 'she has grown pale' and no one says 'he has left her' (துறந்தார் அவர் என்பார் இல்). In 1235 the wasted shoulders themselves declare his cruelty. One speech says the visible change brings talk about her alone, and the other says the same kind of change speaks against him; the difference is in who is reading the body, the town or the friend.

In 1190 the woman says it is good to be called pale, if only they will not proclaim the unkindness of the man who won her (நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்). In 1236 she says that as bangles and shoulders slacken, she is hurt by his being called cruel (கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). In both she accepts the damage to her body and resists blame of him; Parimelazhagar gives both as replies to the friend's faulting of the man.

In 1169 the woman herself speaks of the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமை) when she says the long nights are crueller still. In 1236 she is pained when he is called cruel (கொடியர்). The pair shows that she uses the word in her own lament and does not accept it from another's mouth; these are different moments of a dramatised speaker, not a contradiction in teaching.

In 1200 the woman tells her heart that it wants to tell its great pain to one who is not close (உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய்), and that it might as well fill up the sea. In 1237 she asks her heart whether it will win honour (பாடு பெறுதியோ) by telling the 'cruel' one of the outcry over her wasting shoulders (வாடுதோட் பூசல் உரைத்து). Both address the heart as a possible messenger to him; 1200 dismisses the errand as futile, while 1237, as Parimelazhagar reads it, urges the heart to go, with கொடியார் used as other people's word for him.

In 1162 she says she cannot hide this sickness, and that telling it to the one who caused it brings shame (உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்). In 1237 she asks her heart whether it can gain honour by telling him of her wasting shoulders. The two give opposite values to the same act of telling him, shame in one and possible honour (பாடு) in the other; in 1237 it is the heart and not she herself who would carry the word.

In 1187 the woman says she lay embracing him and shifted a little (புல்லிக் கிடந்தேன் புடைபெயர்ந்தேன்), and at that the pallor could be scooped up. In 1238 the man recalls that when he loosened the arms that held her (முயங்கிய கைகளை ஊக்க), her forehead turned pale (பசந்தது ... நுதல்). The same event, pallor at the slightest slackening of an embrace, is told once by her and once by him.

1186 says pallor watches for a weak point in her husband's embrace (முயக்கற்றம் பார்க்கும் பசப்பு) as darkness watches for a lamp to fail. 1238 gives an instance from the man's memory: he loosened his embracing arms and her forehead paled. The simile of 1186 states the rule, and 1238 shows it happening; Parimelazhagar has the man go on to ask what a real separation will do.

In 1108 the man says that for two who desire each other, an embrace that no breeze can split is sweet (வளியிடை போழப் படாஅ முயக்கு). In 1239 he recalls that when a cool breeze did split their embrace (முயக்கிடைத் தண்வளி போழ), her large cool eyes turned pale. The same words, வளி, போழ் and முயக்கு, return: what was the measure of closeness in union becomes the smallest possible separation and already brings pallor.

1238 says that when he loosened the embracing arms her forehead turned pale. 1240 says the pallor of her eyes itself came to distress (கண்ணின் பசப்போ பருவரல் எய்தின்றே) on seeing what the bright forehead had done (ஒண்ணுதல் செய்தது கண்டு). 1240 depends on 1238 for what the forehead did; Parimelazhagar explains that the eyes' pallor was abashed that the forehead had paled sooner than they did, at a smaller cause.

In 1182 the woman says pallor spreads and rides over her body with the pride (தகையால்) that he was the one who gave it. In 1240 the man says the pallor of her eyes felt distress (பருவரல்) on seeing what her forehead had done. Both give the pallor feelings of its own, pride in one and distress in the other, so that பசப்பு is spoken of as a party to the love and not only its symptom.
